desc:
Each row of contestants is [id, solved, penalty]: a contestant's unique id, the number of problems they solved and their total time penalty in minutes.

Contestants are ranked by these rules, in this priority: more solved problems first; then smaller penalty first; then smaller id first. Return the ids in rank order, best contestant first.

Example: [[1, 3, 50], [2, 3, 40], [3, 4, 100]] gives [3, 2, 1]: contestant 3 solved the most, and contestants 2 and 1 tie on solved problems, so the smaller penalty (40) wins.
constraints: Each row has exactly 3 values and all ids are distinct
hints: You have to order records, not plain numbers. What do you compare, and in which order?
Higher solved is better but lower penalty and lower id are better. The directions differ.
Sort with the key (-solved, penalty, id) and read off the ids.
editorial: This is a multi-key sort. Express each rule as an ascending key: more solved becomes -solved, smaller penalty stays penalty, smaller id stays id. The tuple (-solved, penalty, id) then orders contestants exactly as the statement says, and since ids are distinct there are no complete ties, so the answer is unique.
The sort takes O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space. Counting-style tricks are not needed; the point of the exercise is writing the key with mixed directions correctly.
